Re: 
U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, RIN 2900-AS31, Proposed Rule Change on 
Reproductive Health Services published in the Federal Register on August 4, 2025. 
 
 
Dear Dr. Lieberman, 
 
Women’s Law Project (WLP) is a Pennsylvania-based public interest legal advocacy 
organization working to defend and advance the rights of women, girls, and LGBTQ+ people in 
Pennsylvania and beyond. We leverage impact litigation, policy advocacy, public education, and 
direct assistance and representation to dismantle discriminatory laws, policies, and practices and 
eradicate institutional biases and unfair treatment based on sex or gender.  
 
 
We strenuously disagree with the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) proposed 
reinstatement of the exclusion of abortion coverage and abortion counseling from the medical 
benefits package. Coverage of abortion as a needed medical service for veterans was established 
by the interim final rule published on September 8, 2022. We also oppose the reinstatement of 
abortion exclusions to the Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department of Veterans 
Affairs (CHAMPVA). CHAMPVA serves the spouses, children, survivors, and caregivers of 
veterans, and the interim final rule allows for abortion care in the event of rape, incest, or threat 
to the health of the mother.  
 
 
While it may be the Administration’s contention that the Supreme Court’s decision in 
Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization was intended to prevent so-called federal 
overreach in the arena of abortion care, the health and well-being of this nation’s veterans is 
firmly within the Administration’s wheelhouse. It is the federal government’s sacred duty to 
provide all necessary medical care to those who have proudly and selflessly served in the 
military – failure to do so is a stain upon this nation’s legacy. After all, there are nearly 2 million 
female veterans, making up over 9% of the veteran population, and female veterans have 
unplanned pregnancies at rates similar to the civilian population. “Equitable access to high-

2 
 
quality care for all Veterans is a major tenet of the VA healthcare mission.”1 Equitable access 
means including all care that a veteran might need. 
 
 
To categorize abortion care as not a “needed” medical service is a grave error, and always 
was a grave error. The VA demonstrates a lack of understanding, both of medical facts and the 
reality of many of its constituents, when it asserts that abortion care is not a needed medical 
service; not only is that a relatively recent determination, but other authorities, including the 
Pennsylvania Supreme Court, have held that “abortion is healthcare.”2 In any case, it can never 
be to the benefit of anyone’s health to carry an unwanted pregnancy to term. The VA provides a 
full range of reproductive health care services to both male and female veterans, including 
erectile disfunction treatment to men.3 The proposed rule would exclude from coverage a vital 
medical service needed only by female veterans, denying them equity in their care, equity that 
they are entitled to through their service to this country. 
 
 
Furthermore, some veterans rely exclusively on the VA for their healthcare needs. Those 
veterans with nowhere else to turn depend on the VA to provide for them. Without coverage for 
all abortion care, some veterans with unintended pregnancies, or veterans with non-fatal fetal 
abnormalities or other non-fatal yet high-risk pregnancies, will be denied the abortions they seek, 
and will be forced to continue with their pregnancies. As demonstrated by the Turnaway Study, 
women denied wanted abortions suffer severe consequences in almost every area of their lives.4 
These veterans are more likely to end up in poverty, more likely to not be able to cover basic 
living expenses, more likely to stay with an abusive partner, and more likely to suffer serious 
health issues than their peers who receive the abortion care they seek. A veteran makes a choice 
to serve their country, knowing the sacrifices they must make, and is willing to lay down their 
life in service. In return, with this regulation, their country would not give them a choice about 
whether to end their pregnancy, and hence would force them to suffer these preventable 
consequences.    
 
 
The lone exception for life-threatening pregnancies is not nearly good enough. Pregnancy 
itself is fourteen times more dangerous than abortion.5 Carrying a non-viable pregnancy to term 
can cause severe physical injury to the mother, and even if not, it can and does cause serious 
emotional harm to the mother. And beyond that, carrying any unwanted pregnancy to term 
causes tremendous distress to the person who wishes not to be pregnant. 
 
 
To even suggest that abortion is not a “needed” medical service is absolutely wrong, as 
demonstrated by medical science and by the lived experiences of everyone who has ever endured

an unwanted pregnancy. The VA should not reinstate the abortion coverage exclusion, as doing 
so will harm countless veterans who rely on the VA as their medical provider. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
 
 
Tyler Gillett
